title: Use It or Lose It: How Fathers Got Their Leave
subtitle: In 1974 Sweden gave fathers the right to paid time with a newborn. Almost none of them took it. Twenty years later, one small change in the rules made all the difference.
footer: Story Lesson · Talking About the Future · B2
intention: you'll follow a true story about work, family and fairness, and use a full range of future forms — be about to, be due, will be doing, will have done — to talk about what is coming.
warmup: Who looks after a new baby in your country — and who is expected to? Is that changing?
If a law gave you paid time off for something important, would you take all of it? What might stop you?
Think of a rule that changed how people behave. Why did the rule work when advice didn't?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, work out the word in bold, then reveal. Say your guess out loud first.

items.sent: In many countries, new parents receive months of paid parental leave: time away from work, with pay, to care for a baby.
items.meaning: parental leave (noun) — time off work, usually paid, that a parent takes after a baby is born or adopted.

items.sent: Every employee has an entitlement to four weeks' holiday a year; the law says the company must give it.
items.meaning: entitlement (noun) — a right to have or receive something, especially by law or contract.

items.sent: The scheme gives each parent a quota of ninety days, and neither parent can give their days to the other.
items.meaning: quota (noun) — a fixed share or amount that a person or group is allowed or required to have.

items.sent: A discount is a powerful incentive: it gives people a reason to choose one thing instead of another.
items.meaning: incentive (noun) — something that encourages you to do something, such as money, a reward or a benefit.

vocab.heading: B · How change is measured
vocab.intro: Same method: guess from the sentence, then reveal.

items.sent: The take-up of the new scheme was low: only a few percent of the people who could use it actually did.
items.meaning: take-up (noun) — the number or proportion of people who use something that is offered to them.

items.sent: There has been a shift in attitudes: ten years ago most people disagreed, but now most agree.
items.meaning: shift (noun) — a change in position, opinion or direction, usually a gradual one.

items.sent: Some fathers feared a stigma: they worried colleagues would see them as less serious about their careers.
items.meaning: stigma (noun) — a feeling of disapproval or shame that society attaches to a person or action.

vocab.heading: C · Babies and families
vocab.intro: Three words you can use about family life. Guess, then reveal.

items.sent: Spending the first weeks at home helps a parent bond with the baby — to build a close, loving relationship.
items.meaning: bond (verb) — to form a close emotional connection with someone: bond with, bond over.

items.sent: Their baby is due in March, so they expect the birth sometime that month.
items.meaning: be due (adjective) — expected to happen or arrive at a particular time: The baby is due in March.

items.sent: A caregiver looks after someone who cannot look after themselves, such as a baby or an elderly relative.
items.meaning: caregiver (noun) — a person who looks after children, sick people or older people, paid or unpaid.

story_heading: How Sweden taught fathers to take their leave

story.heading: Part 1 — A law nobody used
paras: In 1974, Sweden did something no country had done before. It replaced mothers' maternity leave with a paid parental leave that either parent could take. On paper, it was equality: a mother or a father could stay at home with a new baby, and the state would pay.

The law was generous, and the politicians were proud of it. But when researchers looked at the numbers, they found a strange result. Fathers hardly used it. At the start, only about half of one percent of all the leave days were taken by men, and for years afterwards the figure stayed very small.

The reasons were not complicated. In most families the father earned more, so the household lost less money if the mother stayed home. Employers expected men to be at work. And many fathers worried about the stigma: would colleagues think they were not serious? The right existed. The take-up did not.
checks: What was new about Sweden's 1974 law?
What was the problem with the results?
Give two reasons why fathers did not use the leave.
answers: It was the first paid parental leave that either parent could take, instead of leave for mothers only.
Almost no fathers used it — only about half of one percent of leave days at the start.
Any two: fathers usually earned more, employers expected men to work, and men feared how colleagues would see them.
story.discuss: Why can a right exist on paper but not in real life? Can you think of other examples?

story.heading: Part 2 — The month that disappeared
paras: For twenty years, Sweden tried persuasion: public campaigns encouraging fathers to share the leave. It helped a little. It did not change much.

Then, in 1995, the government tried something different. It reserved one month of the leave for each parent. If the mother wanted to use the father's month, she could not. If the father did not take it, the family simply lost it. The newspapers called it the "daddy month". The principle was brutally simple: use it or lose it.

The effect was fast. Once the month belonged to fathers, the incentive was clear — and the worry about what colleagues thought grew weaker, because every father was in the same position. Sweden added a second reserved month in 2002 and a third in 2016. Today, each parent has a quota of 90 days that cannot be transferred.

Iceland copied the idea in 2000 with a "3+3+3" model: three months for the mother, three for the father, and three to share. Before the change, men used only a fraction of one percent of the leave. Afterwards, around nine in ten fathers took some.
checks: What did Sweden try before 1995, and did it work?
What was the rule of the "daddy month"?
answers: It tried campaigns and posters; they helped a little but did not change much.
One month of leave was reserved for the father. If he did not take it, the family lost it — it could not be transferred.
Three months for the mother, three for the father, and three the parents could share.
story.discuss: Is it right for a government to make a rule that people cannot change, if the aim is fairness? Where is the line?

story.heading: Part 3 — Did it work?
paras: Researchers who study families have found that the reserved months did more than put fathers at home. In some studies, the longer a father took leave, the more involved he stayed in daily care later on. A man who had spent weeks as the main caregiver, they argue, understands the work in a way that a visitor never does. It also helps him bond with the child early.

But the story is not simply a triumph. Fathers in Sweden still take fewer leave days than mothers — in recent figures, roughly a third of the total — and equality campaigners say progress has slowed. Some couples also feel the state is telling them how to live: why should a family that wants one parent to stay home be punished for it?

Supporters reply that the rule only works because it is firm: a quota that can be swapped is a quota that mothers end up using. Critics reply that fairness cannot be forced. Both agree on one thing. The shift in what people think of as normal for a father has been dramatic. In 1974, a father pushing a pram on a weekday morning would have been an unusual sight. Today it is ordinary.
checks: What do the studies say about fathers who took longer leave?
Give one criticism of the reserved-month rule.
What do both sides agree on?
answers: They tend to stay more involved in daily care of the child later on.
Any one: it limits families' freedom to choose; it can be seen as the state telling people how to live; fathers still take fewer days than mothers.
That the shift in what is seen as normal for fathers has been dramatic.
story.discuss: Which is the stronger argument — "fairness needs firm rules" or "families should choose for themselves"? Why?

grammar.name: Talking About the Future
grammar.lead: A story about a policy is full of futures — what is coming, what will be happening, what will already be finished. English has several ways to look ahead, and each says something different.
notes: 1 · be about to + verb — it is starting right now. “Pack your bag — the taxi is about to arrive.” “The new law is about to come into force.” It means very soon, almost immediately.
2 · be due (to) — it is scheduled or expected. “The baby is due in March.” “The report is due to be published on Friday.” Use it for births, deadlines and timetables.
3 · will be + -ing (future continuous) — in progress at a future time. “This time next month, I will be changing nappies at three in the morning.” It pictures the middle of an action.
4 · will have + past participle (future perfect) — finished by a future time. “By June, I will have used all my leave.” It looks back from a point in the future.
5 · will or be going to? Going to is for plans and evidence: “I am going to take the full month.” Will is for offers and quick decisions: “I 'll hold the baby while you eat.”

6 · The traps. about to arriving → “about to arrive”.  due arrive → “due to arrive”.  will be have finished → “will have finished”.  By Friday I will be finishing it → if it is complete by then, use “I will have finished”.

exercises.heading: Use the form in capitals
exercises.intro: Write the verb in the form shown. Write the full verb phrase.
items: 1. Pack the bag now — the taxi ___ (ARRIVE: be about to).
2. This time next week, I ___ (SLEEP: future continuous) in my own bed again.
3. By the end of March, they ___ (FINISH: future perfect) the nursery.
5. “I can't carry all these bags.” “Don't worry, I ___ (HELP: offer, will).”
answers: 1. is about to arrive
2. will be sleeping
3. will have finished
4. is due (the baby is due in May)
5. will help (or: 'll help)

exercises.heading: Fix the mistake
exercises.intro: Each sentence has one mistake in the future form. Rewrite the whole sentence correctly.
items: 2. I will be have finished the report by Friday.
3. He will took two months of leave next year.
4. She is due give birth in May.
5. She will has finished the report by Friday.
answers: 1. The baby is about to arrive.
2. I will have finished the report by Friday.
3. He will take two months of leave next year.
4. She is due to give birth in May. (or: She is due in May.)
5. She will have finished the report by Friday.

exercises.heading: Write it from the notes
exercises.intro: Write one sentence for each note, using the form in brackets. Then say them aloud.
items: 2. (be due) the new rules / come into force / next January → ___
3. (future continuous) at 9 tomorrow morning / I / travel to the airport → ___
4. (future perfect) by next summer / she / take / all her leave → ___
5. (going to) we / decide / who stays at home / tonight → ___
answers: 1. The meeting is about to start.
2. The new rules are due to come into force next January.
3. At nine tomorrow morning, I will be travelling to the airport.
4. By next summer, she will have taken all her leave.
5. We are going to decide who stays at home tonight.

grammar.closing: Now say three sentences about the next few weeks of your own life: one with be about to, one with will be -ing, and one with will have done.

deeper.heading: Going deeper — fairness, freedom and the rules that change behaviour
deeper.lead: The Swedish story is really an experiment about human behaviour: when does advice work, when do rules work, and who decides what is fair?

blocks.heading: Why "use it or lose it" works
paras: The reserved month changed three things at once. It gave families a financial reason to act. It gave fathers a reason to say to an employer, "This is the rule, not my choice." And it removed a silent conflict inside the couple: neither person had to ask the other to give something up.

Notice what the rule did not do. It did not tell fathers how to feel, how to behave at home, or what to believe. It simply changed the cost of doing nothing. Many policies, from pension schemes to savings plans, use a similar idea: they change what happens if you do nothing.

items.q: Which word means "something that gives you a reason to act"?
What is the rule's main principle, in four words?
Say in the future perfect: “The family will lose the month” (if the father does not take it by his child's first birthday).
items.a: By the child's first birthday, the family will have lost the month.

blocks.heading: Two sides of the argument
paras: People who think carefully about this still disagree.

pairs.b: Without a reserved quota, the leave tends to go to the mother, because of income and expectations. A firm rule gives fathers a safe reason to take it and keeps the system equal.
Every family is different. A couple might prefer one parent at home for a year. A rule that punishes that choice treats all families as if they were the same.

blocks.heading: Language for talking about work and family
paras: Complete each sentence from memory. Then reveal.

items.q: “I'll be ___ (work) from home for the first month.” Which form follows “I'll be”?
“By the time he is back, I ___ (finish) the whole project.” Write the form.
items.a: will have finished — completed before a point in the future.

items.q: “Her baby is ___ in June.” (due / about / going)

discuss: Is it right to use a rule that families cannot change, in order to reach a fair result?
What other situations need “use it or lose it” to change behaviour — saving, health or the environment?
Does a rule like this change how people feel, or only how they act? Does the difference matter?

speak.intro: Now it's your turn. Choose a task, start the timer and talk. Try to use at least three different future forms in each answer.
speak.useful: “… is about to …” · “… is due to …” · “This time next month, I'll be …ing” · “By then, I will have …” · “I'm going to …” · “I'll …” (an offer)

tasks.label: Task 1 — The first week
paras: Picture the first week of a big change — a baby, a new job, a house move. What will be happening, and what will you have done by then?

tasks.label: Task 2 — The month you can't swap
paras: A company offers one extra month of leave, but you lose it if you don't take it. Would you take it? Argue both sides.

tasks.label: Task 3 — Who does what?
paras: How do the people in your family share work, money and care? What is different from your parents' generation?

tasks.label: Task 4 — Advice
paras: Someone is about to start a big new chapter of life. Give them five pieces of advice, with a reason for each.

final: Sweden spent twenty years persuading before it used a rule. Was that time wasted, or did persuasion make the rule possible?
Is a rule that works by taking away a choice still a fair one?
If you were designing a leave policy from scratch, what would you reserve for each parent, and what would you leave open?
From memory: retell the story in five sentences, using "use it or lose it", one future form from the lesson, and the word incentive.
